Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 43
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Vignette:
Clara, forty-three, had come to believe her body was no longer entirely her own. The life-threatening illness that had nearly taken her began on a humid Tuesday during a dinner rush in her restaurant’s prep kitchen. A sudden fever spiked into septic shock, and within hours she was intubated, monitored, and admitted to the intensive care unit. In the present, when the memory surfaces, it does not arrive as a distant story but as a complete sensory reliving. She feels the sterile hospital air on her face, hears the rhythmic hum of the ventilator, tastes the dry cotton of the endotracheal tube, and sees the pale ceiling tiles pressing down. The event is so extreme that it is hard to believe it actually happened to her, and when the recall strikes, a heavy grief settles over her chest. For months after returning to the kitchen, her body reacted to danger before her mind had time to catch up. A draft from the walk-in cooler would tighten her shoulders. A dropped stainless-steel pan made her breath hitch and her pulse jump. She could not relax even when she knew she was safe, lying beside her partner in their bedroom, certain that another wave of fever could arrive without warning. She had come to believe her body was permanently damaged by the illness, a fragile instrument that might fail again. This physical vulnerability sat alongside a quiet negative appraisal: she would never be able to feel normal emotions again. When positive moments occurred—a perfectly timed service, a guest’s compliment, a quiet evening out—she found herself avoiding them. Hope sat beside her, steady but distinct. Emotional numbing settled over her like a heavy apron; she smiled, she cooked, she held her partner’s hand, but the sensations remained distant, carefully kept at bay. Her occupational environment became the stage where these habits formed. Standing at the pass during service, she watched the line cook call out orders and felt her own heart beat ahead of her thoughts. She delayed sleep, staying up until the house was completely dark, watching the digital clock tick past two. The nights offered a quiet rhythm; if she stayed awake, she could watch for danger before it arrived. Over weeks, this habit solidified. The avoidance of positive events grew heavier, particularly in moments that asked her to feel hopeful. A birthday celebration for her partner in their apartment kitchen triggered a sharp surge of warmth, followed quickly by a sudden, overwhelming grief and a racing pulse that made her step back from the table. She was certain that feeling too much meant risking a return to that sickbed. The flashbacks came without warning—a smell of hospital antiseptic drifting from a cleaning cart, the beep of the microwave sounding like a monitor—and she would suddenly act as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, her hands gripping the counter until the moment passed. Clara’s partner noticed the quiet withdrawal, the way she braced herself when laughter filled the room, and how she retreated to the edge of the kitchen island when the service rhythm quickened. It was a recent birthday dinner that finally brought her to seek help. The sudden grief, the body’s premature warning, the persistent inability to settle in a safe space—they had accumulated into a steady weight. She walks into the clinic hoping to understand why her body keeps sounding alarms in a world that feels steady, and what frightened her most was the possibility that she would never again trust her own emotions or her own skin.
